name: Hostile attribution bias
statement: People who behave aggressively are more likely than others to read an ambiguous action by someone else as deliberately hostile.
meaning: The claim belongs to social information processing theory, which treats a social response as the output of several steps: encoding the cues, working out what the other person meant, picking a goal, generating responses and choosing one. Hostile attribution bias sits at the interpretation step. Somebody spills a drink on you, or a ball hits you in the back, and the cause is genuinely unclear. The claim is that aggressive children and adults settle on 'they did that on purpose' more often than other people do. Two things follow, and they are usually run together. One is a correlation between a person's readiness to infer hostile intent and how aggressively they behave. The other is a causal story in which the inference drives the aggression, and so changing the inference should reduce it. The first is well measured. The second is a separate question with much thinner evidence.

origin.note: Dodge's paper, 'Social cognition and children's aggressive behavior', runs from page 162 to page 170 of volume 51. Later work dates the idea to it, and De Castro and colleagues, reviewing the field in 2002, group Dodge's own result with the studies reporting small effects. A second 1980 paper carries the title 'Attributional bias among aggressive boys to interpret unambiguous social stimuli as displays of hostility', by W. Nasby, B. Hayden and B. M. DePaulo in the Journal of Abnormal Psychology. Neither PubMed nor Crossref carries an abstract for either paper.

evidence: Almost all of it is vignette work. A child hears or reads a short story in which a peer causes a bad outcome for them and the peer's motive is left open, then says why the peer did it. The answers are scored hostile or benign, and that score is set against ratings of the child's aggression by teachers, peers or parents. De Castro, Veerman, Koops, Bosch and Monshouwer pooled 41 such studies with 6,017 participants in 2002. Verhoef, Alsem, Verhulp and De Castro repeated the exercise in 2019 on 111 studies, 219 effect sizes and 29,272 participants. Both are syntheses of concurrent measurement rather than of experiments. Dodge and 17 colleagues added the largest longitudinal test in 2015, following 1,299 children with a mean age of 8.3 years in the first year across 12 ecological groups in nine countries. Each child rated 10 ambiguous provocation vignettes in year three, and mothers and children rated the child's chronic aggression in years two, three and four. The experimental evidence sits in the intervention literature. Hudley and Graham randomly assigned 101 African-American elementary school boys to attributional retraining, attention training or no treatment in 1993, and the retrained aggressive boys inferred hostile intent less often, endorsed retaliation less often and were rated less aggressive by their teachers afterwards. Yeager, Miu, Powers and Dweck reported in 2013 that teaching adolescents that personality can change reduced hostile intent attributions in an experiment and reduced attributions and aggressive desires over eight months in an intervention.

replication.headline: Two meta-analyses seventeen years apart put the association at the same modest size, and neither can show which way it runs.
replication.detail: De Castro and colleagues found a weighted mean of r = .17, Z = 11.25, p < .001, with 37 of the 41 effects in the predicted direction. Individual studies ranged from r = -.29 to r = .65 and were heterogeneous, chi-square(40) = 188.37, p < .001. Their fail-safe number was 3,411, meaning that many null studies would have to be missing to overturn the pooled result. Verhoef and colleagues, working on a database more than four times the size, report d = 0.33, SE = .03, t(218) = 12.16, p < .001, 95% CI [0.28, 0.39]. They restate the 2002 result as d = 0.35 for comparison, which is the figure this entry uses in the structured field, since the 2002 paper itself reports r. Between-study differences accounted for 68.90% of the variance in the 2019 analysis, so the pooled figure describes a wide spread rather than a stable quantity. Neither synthesis includes designs that measured attribution and aggression at different times. Dodge and colleagues' nine-country study is the longitudinal check: in every ecological group children reported reactive aggression more often in the vignettes where they had attributed hostile intent, and hostile attribution scores predicted later mother-rated and child-rated chronic aggression with prior aggression controlled.

study.cite: Verhoef, R. E. J., Alsem, S. C., Verhulp, E. E., & De Castro, B. O. (2019). Hostile intent attribution and aggressive behavior in children revisited: A meta-analysis. Child Development, 90(5), e525-e547.

limits: The size of the effect depends on how it is measured, which is the field's oldest complaint about itself. In the 2002 analysis, studies that showed situations as pictures found r = .02, video found r = .09, stories read aloud or by the child found r = .24, and the two studies that staged a real interaction found r = .55. The 2019 analysis reaches the same conclusion from a larger base: real-time interaction with an actual peer gave d = 1.33, but that figure rests on three effect sizes from two studies, and around 98% of all effect sizes came from hypothetical stories. Reliability is patchy. Verhoef and colleagues report that fewer than half the included studies gave a Cronbach's alpha, and that the association was stronger where the measure was more reliable. Controlling for intelligence roughly halves the result, r = .10 against r = .18 in 2002, and De Castro and colleagues say openly that they cannot tell whether intelligence is a confound or part of the causal chain. Girls were badly under-represented in the older literature: one study of the 41 included only girls, and one of the seven clinical studies included any girls at all. In adults the evidence is thinner still. Klein Tuente, Bogaerts and Veling reviewed 25 studies of adults in 2019, found small to medium associations across students, patients and forensic samples, and concluded that because most were cross-sectional and the measures varied in quality, the implications for treatment are preliminary.
misreadings: The finding is correlational, and the widely repeated version of it is causal. Verhoef and colleagues state that their design cannot establish the direction of the relation, and Smeijers, Bulten and Brazil say the same of the wider hostility bias literature. Aggression may build the expectation as easily as the expectation drives the aggression. Theory also predicts that the link should be specific to reactive aggression, the hot response to a perceived threat, rather than to the cold instrumental kind. It is not. Verhoef and colleagues found d = 0.36 for reactive aggression against d = 0.33 for aggression measured as a general construct, with no difference between them, p = .602. The 2002 analysis went the other way from the prediction: the four studies that excluded purely proactively aggressive children reported r = .08, smaller than the r = .19 of the studies that presumably included them, which the authors call the opposite of the expected effect. Martinelli and colleagues' 2018 paper on aggression subtype and gender, often cited here, is a systematic literature review of the field rather than a meta-analysis, and reports no pooled figure. The bias is also not a claim that aggressive people misread everything. It concerns ambiguous situations with a bad outcome for the person themselves, and De Castro and colleagues note Dodge and Frame's finding that the effect appears only when children feel they are personally involved. Finally, treating the attribution as a lever is optimistic. Ciesinski and colleagues pooled 29 randomised trials of cognitive bias modification with 2,334 participants and found Hedges g = -0.23, 95% CI [-0.35, -0.11], for aggression. Trials targeting interpretation bias specifically gave g = -0.27, 95% CI [-0.43, -0.12], across 16 studies, and the authors report that this advantage did not hold once baseline aggression was accounted for.
